content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published a guideline on the use of ferritin concentrations to assess iron status in individuals and populations. This document provides evidence-based recommendations for the clinical and public health use of ferritin as a biomarker for iron deficiency and iron overload. It is intended for healthcare professionals, researchers, policymakers, and program managers involved in nutrition and health interventions. Ferritin is a protein that stores iron and is present in all cells. Low ferritin levels indicate depleted iron stores, while elevated levels may suggest iron overload. Accurate assessment of iron status is essential for diagnosing and managing iron-related conditions in individuals and for guiding public health interventions at the population level. The guideline emphasizes the importance of ferritin in diagnosing iron deficiency in apparently healthy individuals. For children, a ferritin concentration below 12 µg/L is indicative of iron deficiency, while for adults, the threshold is 15 µg/L. In the presence of infection or inflammation, ferritin thresholds are adjusted to below 30 µg/L in children and 70 µg/L in adults. Elevated ferritin levels exceeding 150 µg/L in menstruating women and 200 µg/L in men and non-menstruating women may indicate a risk of iron overload. However, ferritin alone should not be used to diagnose iron overload; further clinical and laboratory evaluations are necessary to determine the underlying cause. Adjustments using correction factors are recommended in such cases to improve the accuracy of iron status assessment. The recommendations in this guideline are based on a systematic review of available evidence, which was graded for quality using the GRADE methodology. The evidence supporting the use of ferritin as a marker of iron status was found to be of low to very low certainty for critical outcomes. Despite this, the guideline development group issued strong and conditional recommendations based on the balance of benefits and harms, values and preferences, resource implications, and feasibility of implementation. The WHO guideline also provides cut-off values for ferritin concentrations to define iron deficiency and risk of iron overload across different age groups and physiological states, including pregnancy. It acknowledges the physiological changes during pregnancy that may affect ferritin thresholds, such as plasma volume expansion and inflammatory responses. This guideline updates and supersedes previous WHO recommendations on ferritin use, including those published in 2001 and 2004. It was developed following rigorous procedures outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development, including evidence retrieval, synthesis, and formulation of recommendations. The guideline also identifies research gaps and outlines plans for future updates. The WHO expresses gratitude to the technical experts, contributors, and financial supporters, including the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, for their role in developing this guideline. It is distributed under a Creative Commons license, allowing non-commercial use with proper citation.
